item.title: Australia's Glenn Maxwell calls time on international career. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Explosive batsman Glenn Maxwell announced his international retirement Tuesday after being overlooked for Australia’s upcoming Twenty20 series against England.

The mercurial 38-year-old, who had not played a Test since 2017, called time on his one-day career last year but kept the door open for T20s.

He has not been picked since the World Cup in Sri Lanka in February, with selectors bypassing him for a series against Bangladesh in June.

Maxwell was again overlooked for the squad named Monday to play England in November, with a host of younger players instead preferred.

“A little bit sad and a little bit inevitable too, but I’m announcing my retirement from international cricket,” Maxwell said on the Final Word podcast.

“We probably had numerous discussions before and after the T20 World Cup,” he added of talks with selectors. “And it was pretty open-ended.

“There wasn’t any pressure from (Australia team management), and we decided to sort of leave the door open.

“There was a couple of series that were coming up (in which) they were going to look to the future, and we saw that in Bangladesh with guys getting their opportunity and performing really well.

“There was a small hope or discussion that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (against England).

“But I can completely understand the direction they’re going with this squad.” Maxwell played 130 T20 internationals, blasting 2,897 runs with a strike rate of 154.42, leaving as Australia’s third-highest run-scorer after David Warner and Aaron Finch.

While he only played seven Tests, he featured in 149 ODIs, crunching 3,990 runs.

Maxwell also called time on his first-class career with Victoria, but will continue with the Melbourne Renegades in the Big Bash League.

“I’m grateful for the time I was able to play for my country,” he said.

“If you had offered me that career when I first walked into the Victoria change rooms in 2009-ish, I would have bitten your hand off.”

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat, Hasan Nawaz named in Pakistan Shaheens squad for Rising Stars Asia Cup. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat and Hasan Nawaz have been included in the 15-member Pakistan Shaheens squad for the ACC Men’s Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026, with Abdul Samad appointed captain for the 50-over tournament to be held in Qatar from Nov 19 to 29.

The Pakistan Cricket Board announced the squad on Tuesday, with the Shaheens set to defend the title they won in the previous 50-over edition in 2023. Pakistan are also the defending champions of the T20 version of the competition, having beaten Bangladesh A in a final decided by a Super Over.

The eight-team tournament will feature two groups of four sides. Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘B’ alongside India A, Nepal and the United Arab Emirates, while Group ‘A’ comprises Afghanistan A, Bangladesh A, Hong Kong China and Sri Lanka A.

The Shaheens will open their campaign against the UAE on Nov 20, before taking on India A two days later and Nepal on Nov 24. Their first match will be played at the University of Doha Science and Technology ground, with the remaining group fixtures scheduled at the West End Park International Cricket Stadium.

All three group matches are day-night fixtures except the opening game, which will be played during the day. The semi-finals are scheduled for Nov 26 and 27, with the final to be held on Nov 29.

Samad will lead a batting group that includes Maaz, Hasan, Haider Ali, Shahzaib Khan, Farhan Yousuf and Shamyl Hussain. Rohail Nazir has been named as the designated wicket-keeper.

The squad also includes three spin options in left-arm spin all-rounder Danish Aziz, leg-spinner Saad Masood and Sufyan Moqim. The pace attack will be led by Mohammad Hasnain and also features Ahmed Daniyal, Akif Javed and Muhammad Imran Randhawa.

Ahmed Daniyal was part of the Shaheens side that won the previous T20 edition, playing a key role as the team clinched the title against Bangladesh A in a Super Over.

Pakistan won the last 50-over edition in Sri Lanka in 2023, beating India A by 128 runs in the final. They were runners-up in the opening two editions in 2013 and 2017 before winning the competition in 2019.

The Shaheens will be aiming to retain their title against a field that includes several of the region’s emerging sides, with a meeting against India A among the key fixtures in the group stage.

item.title: Beyond equality: The unfinished journey of women's rights in Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh's progress should be measured not only by economic growth, but by whether every woman and girl can live safely, learn, earn, speak and participate on equal terms.
A promise that must become everyday reality
Bangladesh has made important gains in girls' education and women's participation in public and economic life. Women work in factories, farms, schools, hospitals, businesses and public institutions; they support families and contribute to national development. Yet progress is not the same as equality. For many women, the ability to make choices about education, work, marriage, safety and public life is still constrained by violence, economic dependence and unequal expectations.
The Constitution provides a clear starting point. Articles 27 and 28 guarantee equality before the law and state that women have equal rights with men in all spheres of state and public life. The challenge is to make those guarantees real in homes, schools, workplaces, online spaces and public institutions.
The evidence on violence cannot be ignored
The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and UNFPA's Violence Against Women Survey 2024, published in October 2025, found that 76 per cent of women had experienced at least one form of intimate-partner violence in their lifetime, while 49 per cent experienced it in the previous 12 months. The survey also found that many survivors do not disclose the violence they experience. These figures are not simply statistics: they represent barriers to safety, health, dignity and equal participation.
A survivor may remain silent because of fear, stigma, financial dependence, pressure to preserve a marriage, concern for children or a lack of confidence that help will be available. Responses must therefore go beyond asking women to report abuse. Police, health services, legal-aid providers, local government and community organisations need to offer confidential, accessible and survivor-centred support. Investigations must be timely, protection must be practical, and accountability must not depend on a woman's income or social influence.
A childhood should not be cut short
Child marriage is another barrier to equality. UNICEF's Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025 preliminary findings report that 47.2 per cent of women aged 20–24 were first married before age 18. Behind this measure are girls whose education may be interrupted and whose choices about health, work and family life can narrow before adulthood.
Preventing child marriage requires more than enforcement after a marriage has been arranged. Families need social protection and economic support; schools must be safe and accessible; girls need quality secondary education and trusted adults to turn to. Community leaders and local institutions should challenge the idea that early marriage is a solution to poverty or insecurity. A girl's future should not be treated as a family burden to be transferred through marriage.
Economic participation must mean real opportunity
Women's economic contribution is substantial, but opportunity remains unequal. The World Bank's Gender Data Portal, using ILO modelled estimates, reports that female labour-force participation in Bangladesh was 38.6 per cent in 2025, compared with 80.4 per cent for men. Labour-force figures do not capture the full value of unpaid care and household work, much of which is performed by women. They do, however, point to a significant gap in participation in paid work and economic activity.
Closing that gap requires safe transport, affordable childcare, fair recruitment and promotion, equal pay for work of equal value, maternity protection, skills training and access to finance. Women working in informal and home-based sectors also need stronger protections. Entrepreneurship programmes should provide more than motivational messages: women need markets, mentoring, digital access, credit on fair terms and control over the income they earn.
Representation is not the same as influence
Women must be able to shape decisions, not merely appear in photographs or occupy positions without authority. Political parties, local government bodies, trade unions, professional associations and public institutions should create transparent pathways for women to lead. That includes protection from harassment and intimidation, fair access to resources, and meaningful roles in policy development.
Young women in particular should be encouraged to participate in community decision-making and public debate. Their presence can broaden the questions institutions ask and the solutions they consider. But representation should be judged by whether women can speak freely, influence priorities and be held to the same standards of accountability as everyone else.
A shared responsibility
Women's rights are not a concern for women alone. Men and boys, families, educators, employers, journalists, religious and community leaders, and public officials all have a role in challenging discrimination. Equality begins in ordinary decisions: whether a daughter is encouraged to continue her studies, whether care work is shared at home, whether harassment is taken seriously, and whether a woman's opinion is respected.
Bangladesh needs measurable commitments: reduce child marriage; strengthen prevention and response to gender-based violence; improve access to justice and support services; expand safe and decent work; and ensure women's meaningful participation in leadership. Progress should be tracked with reliable data and public reporting, including attention to rural women, women with disabilities, low-income households and women facing overlapping forms of exclusion.
The measure of progress
The unfinished journey of women's rights is not about granting special privileges. It is about ensuring that rights already recognized in law can be exercised in daily life. A girl should be able to finish school without being pushed into marriage. A woman should be able to work without harassment, earn without discrimination and seek justice without fear. She should be able to take part in public life without being threatened or silenced.
Bangladesh's future will be stronger when women's safety, freedom and equal opportunity are treated not as optional development goals, but as foundations of national progress. Equality is not achieved when it is promised. It is achieved when women can experience it—in every home, workplace, classroom and institution.
Shejuti Hossain is a writer and human rights activist.

item.title: From climate pledges to youth power: Bangladesh’s opportunity ahead of COP31. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In 2019, a group of law students in the Pacific began asking whether governments could be held accountable under international law for their response to climate change. Six years later, in July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion clarifying states’ climate obligations and responsibilities towards future generations. Young people had helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court.
Yet the money tells a different story. Between 2019 and 2021, youth-led climate justice initiatives received just 0.76% of mitigation-focused funding from some of the world’s largest climate foundations.
The contradiction is stark. Young people can influence international debates and national politics, yet struggle to secure the resources to turn their ideas into action. They are invited to conferences, consulted on policies and celebrated in public campaigns. But how much influence do they have over budgets, institutions and the decisions that determine where climate finance goes?
For Bangladesh, this is more than a question of representation. Generation Z played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape. As the country prepares for COP31, the challenge is to turn that civic influence into lasting institutional change.
Participation must lead to influence
Young people have spent years securing recognition within the UN climate process. YOUNGO, the official constituency for children and youth, gained full status in 2011. COP27 encouraged countries to include youth negotiators in national delegations, while COP28 established the Presidency Youth Climate Champion. At COP30 in Belém, youth consultations engaged thousands of participants.
These are worthwhile steps, but access does not guarantee influence. A conference badge cannot tell us whether young people changed a negotiating position, shaped a policy or influenced a budget. Travel costs, visa restrictions and limited observer places further disadvantage young people from least developed countries, small island developing states and climate-vulnerable communities.
The goal should be to connect participation with decisions, funding and measurable results.
Bangladesh has a foundation on which to build. Its National Adaptation Plan for 2023–2050 provides a long-term framework for climate resilience. Its NDC 3.0, submitted in 2025, includes child-sensitive targets for maintaining essential services during climate shocks. UNICEF has identified it as the first NDC globally to include youth in its measurement, reporting, and verification process.
The International Centre for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD) at Independent University, Bangladesh, has also demonstrated what practical support can achieve. Between 2023 and 2026, its SIDA-supported CAP-RES project trained 100 youth fellows and funded 57 youth-led climate sub-projects, which together directly reached 47,795 people, nearly half of them women. Such experience shows the value of combining training, mentoring and funding with community-level action.
Still, engagement remains fragmented and often dependent on individual projects and donor support. Opportunities are concentrated in urban centres, while young people from coastal areas, haors, chars and hill districts face greater barriers. Indigenous youth, young women and persons with disabilities need more equitable access. The agenda must also extend beyond adaptation to clean energy, mitigation and green skills, which will shape future employment.
Why climate finance misses young people
The problem is not simply a shortage of money. It is also how funding is designed and distributed.
A review of 100 youth-focused climate finance initiatives by the Commonwealth Secretariat and YOUNGO, launched at COP28, found that funding was generally disbursed in small amounts and information about beneficiaries was often inadequate.
Young applicants may lack established financial systems, organisational experience or evidence of results. Funders, however, also impose complex application requirements and short funding periods that can exclude smaller organisations. Conventional lenders may consider early-stage youth enterprises too risky.
Not every climate initiative should be expected to generate revenue. Community adaptation, disaster preparedness and climate research deliver public benefits that may not produce commercial returns. They need grants and public funding, not debt. Concessional loans, guarantees and blended finance have a role where youth-led enterprises have credible business models and realistic repayment prospects.
International commitments provide an opportunity, but access remains a concern. At COP29, developed countries committed to take the lead in mobilising at least US$300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, within a broader call to scale climate finance to US$1.3 trillion a year. COP30 called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035.
For least developed countries, the terms matter as much as the headline figures. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, for example, had around US$250 million available for its first call for proposals, against requests estimated at US$2 billion to US$3 billion.
Least developed countries have also committed, through the LDC Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience, to channel 70% of climate finance to local-level action by 2030. Youth-led initiatives should be part of this effort, supported by accessible funding channels and proportionate accountability requirements.
Turning commitments into action
Bangladesh does not need an entirely new climate finance system. It needs to make existing institutions more accessible and accountable.
First, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should formalise youth representation in NDC 3.0 monitoring, National Adaptation Plan reviews, local climate planning and official COP delegations. Selection should be transparent and geographically representative. Institutions should report annually on which youth recommendations were adopted and explain why others were not.
Second, national financing institutions should establish accessible funding windows. Bangladesh Bank could assess how its young entrepreneurs and green finance mechanisms might support viable youth-led climate enterprises. The Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund, Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation and Infrastructure Development Company Limited should create dedicated funding windows or explicitly include eligible youth-led initiatives in existing programmes.
Third, funding must match purpose. Grants should support research, community adaptation, disaster preparedness and early-stage testing. Repayable finance should be reserved for enterprises with credible cash flows. Mentoring, financial-management support and safeguards against excessive debt should accompany funding, with clear pathways for successful pilots to access further grants, public programmes or investment.
Fourth, the Finance Division and environment ministry should introduce a youth marker in annual climate budget reporting. Development partners and national financing institutions should distinguish commitments from actual disbursements. A regularly updated national mapping of youth climate organisations would help identify funding gaps and measure progress.
Fifth, international climate funds should strengthen Enhanced Direct Access, giving accredited National Implementing Entities the resources and authority to establish locally managed youth grant mechanisms. Simplified procedures should be balanced with appropriate technical support and financial oversight.
Finally, Bangladesh and the LDCs Group should use COP31 to press for an adequately resourced Action for Climate Empowerment plan that strengthens young people’s influence over climate decisions. They should also advocate for more accessible finance for locally led climate action and loss and damage, linked to clear national responsibilities and follow-up.
The opportunity in Antalya
Representation without funding leaves young people unable to act. Funding without transparent selection can reinforce existing inequalities. Both require institutions that explain how youth contributions influence decisions and what funded initiatives achieve.
Ahead of COP31 in Antalya this November, Bangladesh has an opportunity to move beyond expressions of support towards measurable commitments: Formal youth representation, accessible financing and transparent reporting. Its experience in climate planning and locally led adaptation gives it a credible basis for making that case.
Generation Z, which helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court in the Pacific and played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape, does not need another pavilion or another invitation to speak. It needs the authority to influence policy, the resources to put ideas into practice, and the means to hold decision-makers accountable.
Giving young people a genuine share of responsibility is not a symbolic gesture. It is a practical investment in those who will live longest with the consequences of decisions made today.
------------------------------------------------------------
Arif M Faisal is the Director of ICCCAD at IUB. The views expressed herein are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of any affiliated organization

item.title: Seven migrants drown off Canary Islands. [ dawn ]
item.description:
MADRID: At least seven migrants died off Spain’s Canary Islands while more than 380 people were rescued on Monday, the country’s maritime rescue services said.

Two deceased people were found aboard a migrant boat when the coast guard rescued 132 people on Monday, 150 km off Lanzarote. During the same journey, five other migrants had died and been thrown into the sea, authorities added.

Another 250 migrants were rescued by coast guard boats off Lanzarote and the Canary Island of El Hierro earlier on Monday, authorities said. On Sunday, 107 migrants were rescued off El Hierro, according to authorities.

“The worst forecasts are coming true. The Atlantic route is once again claiming lives, this time off the coast of Lanzarote. Behind each one is a life, a story, and a family,” Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo said in a message on X.

The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances.

Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings.

Migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with the same period in 2025, but crossings increased sharply in October, putting additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller and less densely populated ones.

Migrant arrivals in the archipelago have fallen 18pc year on year to 11,527 people, according to the office of the Spanish government’s representative in the Canary Islands.

Asylum seekers deported

Spain has returned to Morocco more than a dozen sub-Saharan African and Asian migrants who reached the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and were turned down for asylum, the first deportation of its kind from the enclave since a mass border crossing in July.

The Interior Ministry said the group had been sent back to Morocco after it agreed to receive them and they remained on Moroccan territory at present. It declined to give numbers or nationalities but migrant and rights charities operating in Ceuta said 16 people from Senegal, Nigeria, Yemen, Cameroon and Bangladesh were deported.

The NGOs claim such returns fail to take into account the risks associated with Morocco’s treatment of migrants from other countries and fly in the face of the values espoused by Spain’s leftist government.

Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher, said Spain’s posture was hypocritical. “Spain, despite its [progressive] speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” she said. “Morocco does not respect many human rights.”

Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026
